feed.title: Combined summary - Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions

entry.title: Combined summary - Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions
entry.summary: Post-quantum migration strategies represent a critical area of focus for cryptocurrency developers, especially as quantum computing advances threaten the security of existing cryptographic systems. The underlying premise involves a future where quantum-safe outputs are available before the anticipated "Q-day," a milestone after which new consensus rules require that legacy outputs can only be spent if they are fully collateralized and satisfy specific criteria, such as time-locks or alternative spending paths. These measures resemble vault or covenant designs, but employ implicit enforcement via soft-fork changes to the protocol. Among the innovative solutions proposed is the "Quantum Landmine" mechanism, which utilizes a commit/reveal scheme designed to penalize theft attempts. In this approach, an owner may hold both legacy and quantum-safe outputs, with the latter acting as a concealed landmine containing proof tied to the owner's legacy private key. After Q-day, spending legacy coins mandates full collateralization and compliance with new restrictions, including time-based limitations and demonstrations of pre-Q-day knowledge. Should a quantum attacker attempt to steal funds by revealing the private key, they encounter a mandatory waiting period prior to accessing the coins. During this interval, the legitimate owner can detect the theft attempt and, by revealing their own proof, claim both their coins and the attacker's collateral. This structure not only deters attackers—who risk the loss of their staked collateral—but also introduces uncertainty regarding which coins are actually vulnerable, thereby increasing overall security. Despite its strengths, the landmine concept faces challenges when many legacy private keys are lost, rendering some outputs unprotected. To mitigate this vulnerability, the "Staked Auction" model has been proposed. Under this system, users stake quantum-safe coins prior to Q-day, offering secret bids to potentially claim stolen legacy outputs. Following Q-day, if a quantum attacker spends a vulnerable output using collateral, an auction period is triggered. Stakers then reveal their bids, and the highest bidder receives a portion of the attacker's collateral, while the original stolen coins are destroyed. This approach enables flexible design choices in terms of bid structures, risk distribution, and collateral management, ensuring that attackers cannot profit unless they outbid all defenders. As a result, attackers are incentivized to act conservatively, and defenders gain additional strategic options. Expanding on these concepts, the "Sats Auction" leverages the dynamics of the Dollar Auction game, described in greater detail in the [Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_auction). Unlike the staked auction, the Sats Auction does not require pre-Q-day commitments. Each legacy coin spend initiates a competitive auction after the landmine timeout, with participants bidding to avoid being the second-highest bidder—a position that results in payment without any reward. This scenario can escalate, causing attackers to lose all their collateral if bidding surpasses the value of the contested output. Notably, original owners can participate, blurring the lines between attackers and legitimate claimants. Variables such as collateral ratios, bid intervals, and the final disposition of forfeited collateral can be tailored, introducing opportunities for economic experimentation and further strengthening defensive mechanisms. The overarching objective of these proposals is to harness incentives and game theory to reduce the risks posed by quantum attacks on legacy coins. While no singular optimal design exists, the flexibility of these mechanisms allows stakeholders to prioritize goals such as complete prevention of attacks, promotion of healthy staking and redistribution, or even randomized outcomes akin to a lottery. Over time, as Q-day recedes into the past, it becomes increasingly likely that spenders of vulnerable outputs are attackers rather than legitimate owners, underscoring the need for adaptable, evolving strategies. Creative application of cryptographic innovation in concert with economic game theory demonstrates the potential to transform quantum threats from a systemic weakness into an opportunity for self-regulation and resilience within decentralized financial networks. These theoretical frameworks invite further exploration and refinement as the community prepares for the realities of a post-quantum landscape.
